items.title: Tailscale SSH Flaws Could Let Hackers Gain Root Access Across Servers From One Compromised Device
items.summary: A new security report warns that Tailscale SSH has flaws that could let a hacker move from one compromised device to root access on other servers. Tailscale SSH lets approved devices log in to each other over a private network. The report, called Tailworm, was published on October 25, 2026, by security researcher Erica Windisch of Cyberdione Labs. Tailscale has not confirmed the findings, and as of the report date, it had published no bulletin, CVE number, or fixed version for them. Tailscale SSH Flaws The report lists 11 findings in five groups. They cover Tailscale’s SSH server, its serve and app connector features, the DERP relay client, and headscale, an open-source server that manages Tailscale networks. The researcher tested tailscale 1.104.2 and headscale 0.29.5 between October 22 and October 24, 2026. # Finding ID Component What breaks Severity What an intruder needs 1 F1 (T3) Tailscale SSH Local socket forwarding (ssh -L) runs as root and reaches root-only sockets. In the lab, this gave root and read /etc/shadow. High An SSH rule that allows local forwarding 2 F2 (T2) Tailscale SSH Remote socket forwarding (ssh -R) replaces root-owned sockets. This allowed root code execution through a command daemon. High An SSH rule that allows remote forwarding 3 F3 (T2-RACE, T3-RACE) Tailscale SSH A timing gap lets a path check be defeated before the file action runs. In the lab, this led to a rogue node joining the network. High Ordinary SSH session with forwarding allowed 4 F4 (C1) App connectors (conn25) A user entitlement allows any outbound destination through the connector. This reached cloud metadata and Kubernetes services. High An ordinary app entitlement 5 F5 (T1) Tailscale SSH Session churn causes the root daemon to run out of memory in a loop. About 536 MB was allocated in 7 seconds. High An authenticated SSH session 6 F6 (C2, C3, C4) headscale and DERP client Unauthenticated registrations can evict pending device approvals. A malicious relay can also force a client to read up to 1.34 GB. Medium-High Internet access to headscale, or a hostile relay 7 F7 (SERVE-F-1) tailscale serve A TCP forward to the local API socket lets a remote peer write to the local API. In the lab, a settings change returned success, which means node takeover. High Serve configuration by the operator, plus an allowed peer 8 F8 (SERVE-F-2) tailscale serve A symlink swapped after setup defeats the socket guard, which allows root dials to root-only sockets. Medium (contained) Local write access to the backend path’s directory 9 F9 (SERVE-F-3) Funnel Funnel access depends only on the peer capability and local settings. The report treats this as a threat-model issue. Medium A funnel-enabled node 10 F10 (SERVE-F-4) tailscale serve The TS_SERVE_ALLOW_ALL_INTERFACES setting exposes serve outside the tunnel bind. The report calls this a configuration note. Configuration note Nodes that set this variable 11 F11 (SERVE-F-5) tailscale serve A race in shared serve context lets one mount’s permissions carry over to another. Medium, or Low-Medium without header authorization Serve setups that use header-based authorization The most serious group involves Tailscale SSH. Its SSH server runs inside tailscaled, a background program with full root power on the machine. According to the report, when a user has permission to forward Unix sockets, which are local channels used by services such as Docker, the program opens or replaces those channels using root rights. In the lab, an ordinary SSH session gained root and read the /etc/shadow password file almost instantly. The researcher also describes a chain that spreads across a network. In the lab, one hacked device reached root on other servers and enrolled a rogue node that looked like a trusted server. The report says this spread needed no passwords or stolen keys, and it moved from device to device in under a second per hop. Tailscale builds a private mesh network in which devices trust each other based on policy rules. According to the report, every device receives a full list of its peers, so a hacker on one machine can see every possible target. The researcher says the first foothold can come from a vulnerable web app, a poisoned software package, a phishing implant, or stolen login details. This matters because the policy assumes that trusted devices are safe. The report says Tailscale does not create the first foothold, but it can turn one small breach into wide access across a fleet. Per-pair access rules stopped the spread in the lab, and the researcher calls them the single control that worked. Threat groups have already used Tailscale to move across networks. A Scattered Spider threat actor profile describes how the group used Tailscale VPN to move across environments. Beyond SSH, the report describes problems in the experimental conn25 app connector feature. According to the researcher, a device with connector permission can send traffic to any destination it picks, including the cloud metadata service that holds server credentials. In Kubernetes clusters, the same path could reach internal services. The report also describes a headscale memory problem that needs no account. The researcher says a remote user can exhaust memory on the control server, which can block new devices from joining. A serve feature can also expose the local admin interface to remote peers when it forwards traffic to a Unix socket. A Pattern of Recent SSH Fixes This is not the first serious Tailscale SSH issue this year. In July 2026, Tailscale fixed TS-2026-009, where a username beginning with a dash could make a Linux account lookup return the root account. That let a user with SSH access open a root session in violation of ACL rules. The fix arrived in version 1.98.9. Root access through SSH is also a wider Linux problem. A Linux privilege escalation report shows how an SSH user with a low-level foothold can reach root on major distributions. The researcher also argues that the open-source design moved away from layered protection. The report says Tailscale SSH replaces OpenSSH, which splits privileges so that user sessions run with the user’s rights. The researcher says OpenSSH drops privileges before a session starts, while the Tailscale path keeps a highly privileged process in charge. No official patch exists yet, so administrators should follow the researcher’s interim steps and Tailscale’s documentation. Replace broad identity-wide or tag-wide SSH rules with per-pair grants that name one source and one destination. Set forwarding to denied in each rule where that setting exists. On headscale 0.29.5, forwarding cannot be turned off, so every SSH grant should be treated as root-equivalent. Turn off Tailscale SSH on devices that do not need it by running tailscale set –ssh=false. Confirm another way to reach the device first, because the documentation warns that you may lose access. () Remove app connector permissions where they are unused, remove serve forwards that point to Unix sockets, and turn on node-key expiry. If a device is compromised, delete it at the control plane, because reimaging the host does not revoke keys that were already copied. Credentials matter as much as code. Tailscale reported that an AI agent used a stolen Tailscale credential to enroll 181 nodes during the Hugging Face intrusion, although Tailscale said no vulnerability was exploited. Readers should review the Tailworm report directly and watch Tailscale’s security bulletins for an official response. Some commenters dispute how severe the findings are, and the results come from lab tests rather than confirmed breaches. Still, the report shows how one compromised device can become a path to many servers when access rules are too broad. Teams that use Tailscale SSH should review their rules today and read Tailscale’s SSH documentation before making changes. Update defenses against new malware as soon as it appears. items.title: Microsoft Teams to Use AI for Detecting Phishing Attacks Using Teams Conversations
items.summary: Microsoft is preparing to add AI phishing detection to Microsoft Teams, using conversation context to spot scams that may contain no harmful links or attachments. The feature will focus mainly on first conversations with external contacts, where attackers can pose as trusted support staff and ask employees to share sensitive information. Microsoft detailed the change in Message Center notice MC1519866 , published on October 21, 2026. Targeted Release is scheduled to begin in early November and finish by mid-November. Worldwide general availability is expected to start in early December and finish by mid-December, rather than reaching every customer in November. How Conversation Context Helps Detect Phishing Traditional warning signs, such as suspicious links and infected files, are not always present in social engineering attacks. A message can instead build trust, claim an urgent account problem, and persuade someone to disclose a password or approve remote access. Microsoft says the new capability will analyze conversation context to identify phishing, impersonation, social engineering, and deceptive intent. Its support guidance describes coverage for individual and group chats involving new external contacts across mobile, desktop, and web. Roadmap entry 575288 lists Android, iOS, Mac, desktop, and web support for the worldwide standard cloud. The warning example accompanying the announcement shows an external account called “MOD Administrator” discussing permission problems before asking, “Can you share your credential first?” Teams displays a notice saying the message could be a phishing attempt. The example illustrates why the meaning of a conversation can matter even without a dangerous URL. Source : Microsoft This addresses a familiar attack pattern. Cybersecurity News previously reported on attackers impersonating IT help desk staff through Teams , using convincing support requests to push users toward malware or remote access. Separate reporting described fake support operators abusing Quick Assist after contacting employees through external Teams accounts. Microsoft says detection may initially run silently while it checks quality. Visible warnings may appear after that validation, so users should not expect every suspicious message to trigger an immediate banner during the rollout. For most users, protection centers on external first-contact chats. Teams mobile users in China may also receive protection for conversations within their own organization, reflecting fraud patterns seen in that region. This is a specific extension, not a promise of universal internal chat scanning. Microsoft states that the capability serves security purposes only. It is not intended for advertising, employee monitoring, productivity analysis, or conversation summaries. Customer message content is not retained by the detection system for model training or other secondary uses. That statement should not be read as a change to all existing Teams retention policies. What Organizations Should Do No new administrator configuration is required to enable the protection. However, Microsoft recommends reviewing guidance for unfamiliar external contacts and encouraging users to report suspicious activity or incorrect detections. When a warning appears, employees should check the sender’s identity and email address through a trusted channel. Microsoft advises blocking and reporting confirmed phishing, while mistaken warnings can be reported as not a concern. Users should never share passwords, verification codes, financial details, or sensitive information through an unexpected support conversation. The update adds another warning layer, but staff still need to independently verify unexpected support requests and report suspicious contacts, rather than treating the absence of a banner as proof of safety. items.title: Is Software Development a “Solved Problem”?
items.summary: The term “Solved problem” refers to a problem that was once without a solution, but at some point a solution was discovered. The solution may or may not be optimal, but if it’s good enough for the problem domain, the problem becomes “solved”. For example, once we didn’t know how to land a spacecraft on the moon, which was an interesting and challenging problem, but now that we do, it’s no longer as interesting. Landing on the moon may be “out there”, so let’s get back to earth. The discipline of Software Development, or Software Engineering if you prefer, has developed somewhat organically into something one can learn. A “junior” software developer may know just one programming language and have no experience with real code bases, while a more “senior” developer may know multiple programming languages, has worked on real code bases, which are messier than one would have liked, and also is familiar with many of the so-called “Design patterns”. Of course, I’m oversimplifying – “junior” vs. “senior” is not about counting programming languages, it’s about depth of understanding, problem-solving ability, technical prowess (“knowing” a programming language has many levels), etc. Here is a simple example. In software development, if you need to sort an array of numbers, you’ll use a well-known algorithm, like Quicksort or Mergesort, to do the job. You won’t even know the exact algorithm, because you’ll use some library that does the work for you; sorting arbitrary numbers is a solved problem. Most developers couldn’t care less about the details; they make the function call and move on. That’s old news. Now developers have AI at their disposal. You can ask the AI to build a feature in your software system, and it will do so. We know AI builds complete websites, including a back-end, a database, and front-end, without the human needing to write or see a single line of code. Is that kind of ability reserved for “simple” systems like websites? In other words, is software development a solved problem? As some of you know, I have written tools, most of them with a GUI (yes, I like GUIs), that are open source on my Github account ( https://github.com/zodiacon ). I have many tools, which means writing all those tools requires a lot of time; I’ve been doing that in my “spare” time for some years now. There are always more features I’d like to add, and bugs I don’t have time to fix (or discover!). In the past few months, I’ve been using Claude Code to add features and fix bugs in my various tools. The result is very good, even impressive. I have managed to add dozens of features and fix many bugs in a fraction of the time it would have taken me to do the work manually. Tools like Total PE, Total Registry, Object Explorer, WFP Explorer, to name a few, have benefited greatly. Not only that, my WTLHelper library that I created to provide Windows Template Library (WTL) functionality that is reusable across projects grew significantly, including having a good hex editor/viewer control, a Graph control (like Task Manager’s Performance graphs), and even a Graph/Node/Edge control (in the computer science sense). The Graph controls were built without me writing a single line of code, and they work great. As another example, I always wanted to build a Process Explorer/System Informer style tool, but with my personal “touch”. I did that partially with “System Explorer”, and more recently with “TotalSystem”, an Imgui-based tool, but Imgui is not the best library for this kind of tool (IMHO). I wanted a WTL-based tool, with dark mode (considered “basic” now), and all sorts of information, graphs – the works. So I decided to use Claude to do that without writing code myself (except the base WTLHelper, which I have written already, and Claude improved) and a WinSys library I’ve been working on (and Claude added to as needed). I did that in a few days of Claude working and me guiding. It’s called WinSysLive ( https://github.com/zodiacon/WinSysLive ), and it’s really impressive (at least I think so). I considered changing the copyright notice to “(C)Pavel Yosifovich and Claude Code” – I certainly can’t claim I’ve written all the code – it was mostly written by Claude. Here are some screenshots: These achievements convinced me that software development in general is a solved problem. Obviously, I can only speak for myself. The state of AI coding agents, even today (and they will get better), showed me that the way software developers used to work just a couple of years ago is gone. Software should now be designed by humans, possibly requiring a detailed document for complex systems. Just like software development is iterative, so is the new way of working. Humans write a design in natural language, specify constraints as needed, and then hand it off to the AI to implement. If there are bugs in functionality or design, the AI will fix them. The design document may be modified (requirements change), and the AI will update the code. I believe that looking at the code by a human is no longer necessary in the vast majority of systems. There are always edge cases, niche domains, and unique constraints in terms of CPU, memory, etc., which the AI may not get right the first time. It may need a “push” from an expert human. Experts are still needed, but probably less so, although still as valuable as ever, if not more so. In fact, being an expert will be truly unique, as mainstream developers may be “losing their touch”, getting farther and farther from the details. It will be fine for the majority of work. But from time to time, expert help would be required. Just like Star Trek I like the Star Trek universe, especially how it’s portrayed in “The Next Generation” TV show. The relatively utopian world portrayed is what humanity should strive for. No more chasing money as a prime motivation. Research, discovery – that’s where the challenges lie. But I digress. In the Star Trek universe, the Computer entity is just like today’s AI – engineers talk to it to get things done. They can always intervene, but all the basics are covered by the computer without human intervention. Obviously, Star Trek is simplified in terms of computers and software, but the general idea is valid. Programming languages will no longer matter; I would argue that even now they matter less and less, as the AI interacts with the code more than humans. We even have the AI do code reviews on its own code, with a different “skill”, a different part of its brain, so to speak What about Software Developers? Where does that leave software developers? Software developers will become designers, guiding the AI, but staying out of the nitty-gritty implementation details for the most part. There will always be exceptions, but by and large, software development as practiced up until several years ago is going away. Does that mean we need fewer developers? I don’t think so. We can do much more with AI tools, work at a higher level of abstraction, and get to new heights. Writing a spreadsheet application will no longer be a challenge – the AI can do that on its own; just tell it to clone Excel, and you’re done. I mentioned that I “wrote” a node-graph control in a couple of hours, including unit tests and a demo application. I can add more features as I please. That’s the way it’s going to work. Writing generic applications like word processors, calculators, even full-blown operating systems is within AI’s reach. What then? Some companies are built around their software products, say Adobe with Photoshop, Illustrator, etc. Their IP is tied to these applications, perhaps based on the premise that someone else won’t be able to create such applications with the same feature set in a reasonable time. I don’t think this is true anymore. You can create such applications with AI; even if these don’t provide 100% feature parity initially, that may still be good enough to drop these expensive applications. That’s bad news for all similar companies built around generic software products. The industry will change. What does the Future hold? Obviously, I don’t know The advances we see using AI in chemistry, medicine, energy, etc. are where the real future should be. Let’s use AI to cure cancer; build a spacecraft capable of interstellar travel; create cheap and clean energy sources; create a super-secure OS without productivity loss; find ways to grow crops more efficiently; the list goes on, and software is an integral part of all of that. Writing a custom database engine? A drawing program? Even an interpreter for a Domain Specific Language (DSL)? These are solved problems, more or less. Let the AI do that. These are tools that enable building something greater for a better world. Let’s focus on that.

The discipline of Software Development, or Software Engineering if you prefer, has developed somewhat organically into something one can learn. A “junior” software developer may know just one programming language and have no experience with real code bases, while a more “senior” developer may know multiple programming languages, has worked on real code bases, which are messier than one would have liked, and also is familiar with many of the so-called “Design patterns”. Of course, I’m oversimplifying – “junior” vs. “senior” is not about counting programming languages, it’s about depth of understanding, problem-solving ability, technical prowess (“knowing” a programming language has many levels), etc.

Here is a simple example. In software development, if you need to sort an array of numbers, you’ll use a well-known algorithm, like Quicksort or Mergesort, to do the job. You won’t even know the exact algorithm, because you’ll use some library that does the work for you; sorting arbitrary numbers is a solved problem. Most developers couldn’t care less about the details; they make the function call and move on. That’s old news.

Now developers have AI at their disposal. You can ask the AI to build a feature in your software system, and it will do so. We know AI builds complete websites, including a back-end, a database, and front-end, without the human needing to write or see a single line of code. Is that kind of ability reserved for “simple” systems like websites? In other words, is software development a solved problem?

As some of you know, I have written tools, most of them with a GUI (yes, I like GUIs), that are open source on my Github account (https://github.com/zodiacon). I have many tools, which means writing all those tools requires a lot of time; I’ve been doing that in my “spare” time for some years now. There are always more features I’d like to add, and bugs I don’t have time to fix (or discover!). In the past few months, I’ve been using Claude Code to add features and fix bugs in my various tools.

The result is very good, even impressive. I have managed to add dozens of features and fix many bugs in a fraction of the time it would have taken me to do the work manually. Tools like Total PE, Total Registry, Object Explorer, WFP Explorer, to name a few, have benefited greatly. Not only that, my WTLHelper library that I created to provide Windows Template Library (WTL) functionality that is reusable across projects grew significantly, including having a good hex editor/viewer control, a Graph control (like Task Manager’s Performance graphs), and even a Graph/Node/Edge control (in the computer science sense). The Graph controls were built without me writing a single line of code, and they work great.

As another example, I always wanted to build a Process Explorer/System Informer style tool, but with my personal “touch”. I did that partially with “System Explorer”, and more recently with “TotalSystem”, an Imgui-based tool, but Imgui is not the best library for this kind of tool (IMHO). I wanted a WTL-based tool, with dark mode (considered “basic” now), and all sorts of information, graphs – the works. So I decided to use Claude to do that without writing code myself (except the base WTLHelper, which I have written already, and Claude improved) and a WinSys library I’ve been working on (and Claude added to as needed). I did that in a few days of Claude working and me guiding. It’s called WinSysLive (https://github.com/zodiacon/WinSysLive), and it’s really impressive (at least I think so). I considered changing the copyright notice to “(C)Pavel Yosifovich and Claude Code” – I certainly can’t claim I’ve written all the code – it was mostly written by Claude. Here are some screenshots:

These achievements convinced me that software development in general is a solved problem. Obviously, I can only speak for myself. The state of AI coding agents, even today (and they will get better), showed me that the way software developers used to work just a couple of years ago is gone. Software should now be designed by humans, possibly requiring a detailed document for complex systems. Just like software development is iterative, so is the new way of working. Humans write a design in natural language, specify constraints as needed, and then hand it off to the AI to implement. If there are bugs in functionality or design, the AI will fix them. The design document may be modified (requirements change), and the AI will update the code. I believe that looking at the code by a human is no longer necessary in the vast majority of systems. There are always edge cases, niche domains, and unique constraints in terms of CPU, memory, etc., which the AI may not get right the first time. It may need a “push” from an expert human. Experts are still needed, but probably less so, although still as valuable as ever, if not more so. In fact, being an expert will be truly unique, as mainstream developers may be “losing their touch”, getting farther and farther from the details. It will be fine for the majority of work. But from time to time, expert help would be required.

Just like Star Trek

I like the Star Trek universe, especially how it’s portrayed in “The Next Generation” TV show. The relatively utopian world portrayed is what humanity should strive for. No more chasing money as a prime motivation. Research, discovery – that’s where the challenges lie. But I digress.

In the Star Trek universe, the Computer entity is just like today’s AI – engineers talk to it to get things done. They can always intervene, but all the basics are covered by the computer without human intervention. Obviously, Star Trek is simplified in terms of computers and software, but the general idea is valid. Programming languages will no longer matter; I would argue that even now they matter less and less, as the AI interacts with the code more than humans. We even have the AI do code reviews on its own code, with a different “skill”, a different part of its brain, so to speak

What about Software Developers?

Where does that leave software developers? Software developers will become designers, guiding the AI, but staying out of the nitty-gritty implementation details for the most part. There will always be exceptions, but by and large, software development as practiced up until several years ago is going away. Does that mean we need fewer developers? I don’t think so. We can do much more with AI tools, work at a higher level of abstraction, and get to new heights. Writing a spreadsheet application will no longer be a challenge – the AI can do that on its own; just tell it to clone Excel, and you’re done. I mentioned that I “wrote” a node-graph control in a couple of hours, including unit tests and a demo application. I can add more features as I please. That’s the way it’s going to work.

Writing generic applications like word processors, calculators, even full-blown operating systems is within AI’s reach. What then? Some companies are built around their software products, say Adobe with Photoshop, Illustrator, etc. Their IP is tied to these applications, perhaps based on the premise that someone else won’t be able to create such applications with the same feature set in a reasonable time. I don’t think this is true anymore. You can create such applications with AI; even if these don’t provide 100% feature parity initially, that may still be good enough to drop these expensive applications. That’s bad news for all similar companies built around generic software products. The industry will change.

What does the Future hold?

Obviously, I don’t know The advances we see using AI in chemistry, medicine, energy, etc. are where the real future should be. Let’s use AI to cure cancer; build a spacecraft capable of interstellar travel; create cheap and clean energy sources; create a super-secure OS without productivity loss; find ways to grow crops more efficiently; the list goes on, and software is an integral part of all of that. Writing a custom database engine? A drawing program? Even an interpreter for a Domain Specific Language (DSL)? These are solved problems, more or less. Let the AI do that. These are tools that enable building something greater for a better world. Let’s focus on that.

items.title: lighting the skies
items.summary: Someone stated in the early days of the war, a feeling that was reciprocated by the soldier in khaki and the sailor in blue, that a mechanical device would be the determining factor in ending the world conflict, favorably, of course, for the United States and her allies. 1 One of my common topics is the history of nuclear weapons . The "atom bomb" is a rich vein of history because its impact has been as much cultural as technical. Dramatic depictions like Christopher Nolan's Oppenheimer have recently enforced, perhaps even revived, the perception of nuclear weapons as an innovation that forever changed warfare. More quietly, historians and strategists tend to wonder if that is still true today, or if it was ever as true as was supposed—the conventional firebombing of Tokyo probably claimed as many victims as the nuclear attacks on Hiroshima and Nagasaki, for example. Besides, it's not unusual to hear people overstate the significance of nuclear weapons to WWII in a way that is obvious with a brief inspection of the timeline. The technology became available only very late in the war, and for that reason if no other, it must have had less of an impact on the outcome than other revolutionary wartime developments like radar. Why is it that radar, a complex technology that fundamentally changed the landscape of aerial combat, seems so pedestrian? Perhaps because the technology has far more non-military applications, and so is more familiar to our everyday lives. Perhaps because the development of radar was scattered between countries and institutions without the involvement of such intriguing figureheads as J. Robert Oppenheimer (although one wonders if this is because we have not looked as close; certainly radar figures like Henry Tizard had colorful lives as well). Perhaps because radar just isn't as exciting: it does not put on anything like the show of a nuclear detonation. Today, we consider another such step in military technology. This is an invention that forever changed the battlefield, and it's one that does put on a show. In fact, that has become the technology's main purpose. From the 1870 siege of Paris to the modern used car lot, searchlights have marked many of history's great conflicts—and great deals. The concept of electric light has been known since the very early 19th century. An electric arc lamp, or at least one of their ancestors, was demonstrated in 1806. Because of the widely known story of Thomas Edison's incandescent lamp, most people know that electric light had a very difficult journey from idea to practical device. That path was not as simple as what we are taught in schools: besides the several other inventors with a good claim to the lightbulb, incandescent lights were just one of a few technologies that developed in parallel. Before controlled incandescence, the principal form of electric light was still an arc. Arc lamps also did not fall to incandescent bulbs as quickly as you might think. Arc lamps remained the preferred choice for very bright, high-CRI lighting into the mid-20th century, and reached what will likely remain their ultimate form in the late 1960s, as the 15 kW Xenon arc lamps used by IMAX projectors . Along the way, arc lamps displaced many of the early forms of artificial lights: Oxy-hydrogen candles, known as "limelights," fell out of theatrical use. "Moonlight towers" began the displacement of gas lights for street lighting. And the military—the military readily adopted this new form of reliable, practical, powerful lighting. Calling In Light The effect of artificial lighting on military tactics could fill a book. I will focus on one narrow part of this story, but it will be helpful to set the stage with a few of the earlier developments. For much of the pre-electricity era of military history, artificial lighting was mostly a disadvantage. Fires, torches, and other practical sources of light were bright enough to reveal one's location but not bright enough to search anyone else out. Ironically, the main interest that military researchers had in light was often to suppress or conceal it. The chemical light technology developed for theaters and displays had promise, though. One of the first recorded uses of a powerful light for a military venture (and, as far as I can tell, the very first recorded use of a searchlight) came in the context of the American Civil War. The Union Navy sought to economically attack the Confederacy by maintaining a persistent blockade on southern ports; the Confederacy sought to maintain trade, often by sending out "blockade runners" under cover of night. A Union ship, perhaps frustrated by firing aimlessly into the dark, improvised: a theatrical light was mounted to a crude reflector, forming the first naval searchlight. It wasn't a very good one, it was dim and unfocused and the sailors struggled even to keep it lit under maritime conditions. It was good enough, though. By first following the sound, and then casting the light, the Union ship was able to engage the Confederate vessel even on a moonless night. Amusingly, while this incident is widely described in histories of military signals and lights, I have found none that state the outcome. Perhaps it was unfavorable to the victors. Electric arc lamps were far more suitable to military use: simpler to operate (although not as simple as we might today expect), more flexible in their placement, and by the end of the Civil War brighter. The 1870 Siege of Paris, part of the Franco-Prussian War, was a bellwether in the history of military aviation. Cut off on the ground, the French made extensive use of balloons (a technology they had pioneered in the 18th century) to move people and mail. In the process, several records for aerial travel were set. The French enjoyed air superiority and had little need for air defense, but the situation on the ground was much more troublesome. Prussian forces mounted lengthy artillery bombardments, causing devastation limited mostly by the range of their cannons. For the soldiers manning Paris's fortifications, it was important not only to keep attackers outside of the city, but to keep them as far away as possible. Paris, not for nothing known as the "City of Light," had seen demonstrations of arc lamps back to 1850. The invention of the arc regulator (which advanced the carbon rods to keep the arc intact) and improved batteries made the lights more practical by 1870, and during the early days of the siege "electricians" were hastily recruited to the city's defense. They manned a variety of arc lamps installed around the city, limiting the cover of darkness for nighttime assaults. At the summit of Montmartre hill, a position with a clear view over one of the most vulnerable parts of the city's defense, they installed one of the most impressive lights ever built. Not only was it larger than the others, it could operate for longer: the power supply was not a battery, but a dynamo powered by a steam engine. Besides that leap into modern design, the Montmartre light also presents an early example of "tipping and cueing" in intelligence gathering. French intelligence agents, having caught wind of a surprise attack, sent a message to Montmartre where the light's skilled operators aimed it by heading and elevation before applying power to catch the enemy in quite a compromising position. A decade later, the military searchlight had become a standard technology. The Royal Navy regularly equipped ships with dynamo-powered, carbon-arc searchlights starting around 1882. They found that, besides their role in aiming weapons, searchlights could be something of a weapon on their own. Aiming searchlights back at coast defense artillery positions not only exposed them to incoming fire, it also dazzled the gunners and frustrated their efforts to accurately aim at the ships. This principle was memorably demonstrated by a 1903 US joint maneuver exercise, in which the Navy's Atlantic Fleet mounted a simulated attack on Long Island Sound. All together, on cue, the ships trained their searchlights on the main defensive battery at Fort Michie. The soldiers at the fort didn't manage a single shot, they were so blinded by the lights—and limited in their ability to even move around the battlements, since they could so plainly be seen (and fired upon). As the military developed searchlights, they were quickly applied to civilian use. Limited availability of electricity, and limited need for such powerful lighting, meant that searchlights wouldn't yet become part of the urban landscape. They were reserved for special events, especially those with an emphasis on technical demonstrations. Of course, such events were bounteous around the turn of the century in the form of various world fairs and expositions. Perhaps the first use of searchlights as a device for entertainment came at the 1893 Chicago World's Fair, which was extensively lit by electricity. A total of 17,000 horsepower of steam engines (so, yes, presumably steam horsepower, a curiously different unit from the one we are familiar with today) powered thousands of arc lights. Most of these were for illuminating the fairgrounds and its many monuments, but some were installed for the sake of light itself. On the roof of the Liberal Arts Building, a searchlight claimed to be the most powerful yet made could light a newspaper well enough to comfortably read at a distance of eight miles. Of course, it was more than just a book light—it was a way to attract attention. Unlike the military context, civilian searchlights were deployed specifically to be seen. Rooftop searchlights became a common feature of large expositions, and by lazily searching the sky they established an atmosphere while guiding curious onlookers to the site of the event. Even this early, it was known that searchlights could be a powerful form of advertising. At the Chicago World's Fair, the upstart Cloud Projector Company demonstrated a searchlight with a lens system that could focus a slide onto the cloud layer. It was literally a cloud projector, in the modern sense, and giant words floating ethereally in the sky announced the fair's upcoming special events. In 1901, the Pan-American Exposition was underway at Niagara. Among the attractions was a demonstration of electrical arcs produced by a 40 kV transformer recently installed at the Niagara Falls power station. Alongside that light show, a second, more controlled form of arc was displayed: searchlights. These were described as an application of military technology, and specifically of military signaling technology. Searchlights were installed atop the "Electric Tower" at the exposition grounds, and at a viewing tower erected at Niagara Falls proper. At night, the two lights—22 miles apart—were each plainly visible from the other tower. The military was, of course, well aware of this potential use and as soon as searchlights had been installed on Navy ships they came into use as a means of communication. Extensive newspaper coverage of the Exposition means that we know more details of these machines. The searchlights used for the tower demonstrations had 30" reflectors, and consumed 80 amps at about 50 volts for 4 kW give or take. This was indeed a very bright light for the time, and at the Exposition, the searchlights were swung around among various targets. "As the beams of the projectors sweep across country," The Virginian-Pilot wrote, "the residents of the villages and country places will enjoy the illumination." Excitement for the lights was such that newspapers throughout the region published Morse code tables, in the hope that anyone in the region could decipher news bulletins that were sent from the signal lights. Watching the Skies Electric light is far from the only invention to make a dual appeal to spectacle and the military. From the Wrights' first controlled flight in 1903, it only took about seven years for the Navy to envision the aircraft carrier. The 1911 Italo-Turkish war featured armed biplanes, and as the hostilities of the First World War opened the US Army flew airplanes into Mexico, in pursuit of Pancho Villa. In 1915, the Austro-Hungarian Aviation Troops bombarded the Serbian city of Kragujevac from biplanes. Serbian soldiers fired on them with small arms, but had no success. A private, though, got a lucky shot with an artillery gun. This was the first instance of ground-air combat, and the first use of air defense. By the latter part of WWI, aircraft were in routine use as both bombers and fighters. One tended to lead to the other: our 1915 takedown notwithstanding, bombers and reconnaissance planes enjoyed almost complete freedom of the skies in the first few years of the war, until Germany's fighters presented meaningful resistance. Ground-based air defense lagged behind, but in an interesting turn of aviation history, the held-over use of tethered balloons as observation posts provided a key motivation for improved anti-air artillery. These balloons were conspicuous and almost defenseless, so ground-based escorts accompanied them. Balloons—and in the case of the Germans, Zeppelins—remained an important part of WWI air units. Besides their ability to hang around for an extended period of time, airships could carry much larger payloads than early bombers. Zeppelins occasionally loomed over London, raining down the era's most sophisticated destruction, from 1915 to 1917. These lumbering vessels had their vulnerabilities, though. Big, slow, and flammable, they were easy to take out with artillery fire if you could spot them. German air raids were conducted at night, and by the end of the war Zeppelins were being painted a non-reflective black. By 1916, a network of 258 searchlights across England hunted the skies for airships. There were as many anti-aircraft guns, using the pencil-beams of the searchlights as aiming guides. Air defense was so new at the time that little military doctrine had developed around it, and Britain's first searchlight units were found in the Royal Engineers. As in France, the searchlight operators were known as electricians, specifically the Electrical Engineers. These units had actually formed prior to the outbreak of WWI, for the purpose of coastal defense. None other than Chief Scout Lieutenant-General Robert Stephenson Smyth Baden-Powell (yes, the 1st Baron Baden-Powell) had improvised the use of a chemical searchlight to keep ships away from a besieged town during the Second Boer War; the Electrical Engineers had relieved the use of chemical lights in South Africa when they arrived with arc lights. By 1914, the Electrical Engineers had six companies in London as part of the Territorial Army. With the outbreak of the World War they were immediately put into service, as were other Anti-Aircraft Searchlight companies across Britain. Soon, other companies were deployed closer to the front in Europe. 1910s carbon arc search lamps were not always easy to operate. Most military searchlights by that time were built on the back of trucks, with combustion engine dynamos as a power supply. A typical WWI searchlight unit had three lights, five trucks, and 28 soldiers. Searchlight units became a natural home for other air defense technologies then under development, so that by the end of the war some units had acoustic reflectors (for detecting aircraft by sound) as well. One of the lessons learned during the First World War was that searchlights were quite flexible. Portable searchlights could be used for air-defense, or could be positioned on a hill to light the battlefield (and even dazzle attackers). A technique called "artificial moonlight" took advantage of the enormous output of carbon arc lamps by pointing a searchlight up at clouds and letting the clouds reflect the light back to earth. This dim illumination could help an infantry unit move at night; commanders had the moon on demand. On the other hand, searchlights were vulnerable. Experiments in mounting searchlights on airships to light the ground were of limited success, the lights made the position of the airship obvious and it would quickly be shot down. Similarly, as air-ground combat techniques evolved, searchlights became the first target for incoming enemy aircraft. Destroying the searchlights meant that anti-air guns were firing blind. Even after the First World War established searchlights as a defensive technology—their sweeping beams portending destruction—the public didn't lose its affection for a bright display. In an apparent homage to the use of arc lamps for both stage plays and film projectors, Hollywood's Egyptian Theater had searchlights atop its facade from its opening day. Perhaps inspired by the 1895 installation of an ex-Chicago World's Fair searchlight in Pasadena, the Egyptian Theater's lights announced premieres by sweeping the sky—promotional searchlights learned from air defense, and ironically, the post-WWI fashion for major events was to aim lights upwards, rather than downwards at terrain as had predominated before the war. Grauman extended the concept to his other theaters, with both permanent and portable lights often used at the Chinese Theater. In 1930, for the opening of Howard Hughes's "Hell's Angels," 200 searchlights lined Hollywood Boulevard. The scene could have easily been mistaken for a major air raid, but instead it became part of Hollywood culture. Three years later, 20th Century Pictures adopted its memorable emblem, surrounded by beams of light. Hollywood's searchlights spread beyond just theaters. In 1931, Fisher Motors De Soto-Plymouth on Hollywood Boulevard opened under sweeping lights. Auto dealerships always wanted attention, and searchlights were the perfect combination of electrical modernity, show business spectacle, and mystery. Synchro Searchlights Searchlight technology advanced incrementally between the First and Second World Wars. Carbon-arc lamps remained the underlying technology, but features like automatic carbon regulators (that "fed" the carbon rods towards the arc as they burned away) and foot switches for easy control became standard. A common searchlight at the beginning of WWII might range from 8 to 24 kW, and by the end of the war the largest units reached over 100 kW. The greater innovation of that war was the integration of searchlights into electromechanical fire control systems. New electrical technology, specifically a clever device called a "synchro" or "selsyn," revolutionized searchlight units. A synchro is a way of electrically transmitting a position. Two devices, similar to AC motors, are coupled by a three-phase circuit such that rotating one will rotate the other in proportion. The two "ends" of the synchro will always have the same relative position, so that by putting a synchro transmitter in one place and a synchro receiver in another, you can remote control the position of a device like a searchlight. Synchros were immediately applied to "distant electric control," still a common term in marine searchlights. One of the main problems with the searchlight has always been its tendency to attract enemy fire. Early searchlights often had two operators sitting on chairs to the back or side, cranking wheels for azimuth and elevation. These two operators were often killed early in the engagement. By the use of distant electric control, a searchlight's operators could hide some distance from the searchlight or even operate it from a fortified position like a bunker. This turned out to be a superior way of using a searchlight anyway: operators directly beside later searchlights were practically blinded by the light reflected back by dust and vapor in the air. An operator some distance to the side had a much easier time seeing what was at the end of the beam. Many US air defense searchlights offered a backup, as well: a control crank at the end of a metal arm, called an extended hand control. Were the electrical control system to fail, a searchlight operator could at least stand ten or so feet off to the side and be that much further from incoming fire. Practical use of searchlights for air defense by WWII required adaptation to the better ground-attack capability of aircraft. Searchlights might be stored in a concrete bunker and rolled out on tracks for use, by soldiers who would quickly retreat from the searchlight to a hidden control point. If the searchlight was struck, the operators at least survived, and a well-equipped unit would have a second light ready to go. The purpose of the concrete searchlight shelters was mostly to ensure that a "spare" searchlight would survive the shrapnel from an attack on the one in use. The synchro could also integrate searchlights with other air defense equipment. Early in WWII, radar had not yet been fielded, and acoustic locators remained the state of the art. But they were now part of a unified system: two operators on a set of acoustic listening horns would spin cranks to adjust horizontal and vertical position until the sound of an airplane's engines was loudest. By synchros, this position was transferred to a searchlight control station. These stations resembled a large pair of binoculars on a sort of articulated mount. The base of the control station had readouts for the azimuth and elevation from the acoustic locator, and the operator started by turning wheels to aim the remote searchlight where the locator indicated an aircraft should be present. Once the aircraft was caught in the beam, the searchlight operator threw a transfer switch that placed the searchlight under control of the synchros in the articulations of the binocular mount. From this point on, they tracked the aircraft through the binoculars, and the searchlight followed automatically. The azimuth and elevation from the binoculars could be sent by yet other synchros to readouts at an anti-air control station or even directly to a firing computer that aimed guns. All of this required adjusting for the different locations of each of these components. A combination of old fashioned fire control techniques (placing each station along a common base line) and analog computers did that trick, already well-established technologies since similar computations were needed to aim guns in consideration of gravity and wind. Speaking of a common baseline, it is also worthwhile to discuss the use of searchlights in coast defense during WWII. For a period of the war, the US feared a naval attack, particularly on the West Coast. Similar systems were widely deployed for firing artillery at attacking ships. A set of observation stations, placed along a common baseline, took azimuth readings to enemy ships. Those readings were reported by messenger, and later transmitted by synchros, to a plotting room where a mechanical and later analog computer determined the position of the ship. Yet other computers, at fire control points, determined how to aim the guns. Because this whole system relied on baseline stations visually spotting ships through theodolites, it was much less effective at night. Searchlights were added to many installations, remote controlled by synchros from the baseline stations. Like the azimuth-indicating spotting scopes, two searchlights trained on a ship from a well-surveyed baseline gave enough information to compute a firing solution. Advancing technology obsoleted the whimsical acoustic locating horns. Infrared heat detectors, looking much like searchlights but operating more or less in reverse, were the first electronic means of detecting aircraft in the night. They soon gave way to the first radar sets. The SCR-268, introduced in 1940, was the US Army's first fielded radar system. Its huge beam antenna had three operators on a bench hanging from the back, spinning cranks to adjust the antenna position until oscilloscopes showed the strongest possible return. The SCR-268 was a drop-in replacement for the acoustic locators in searchlight units, but it was far more effective. Skilled radar operators could place an aircraft accurately enough that it was centered in the searchlight beam before the light was turned on. Besides giving enemy pilots quite a surprise, this gave them little time to evade or return fire before anti-aircraft guns were zeroed in from the searchlight. The British developed a more refined version of the SCR-268 called the Searchlight Control Radar. It is notable for its far more compact design, small enough that its antennas were mounted directly to the searchlight under control. The result is almost cyberpunk, a 1.5 meter light bristling with antennas, operators hanging from the sides. The SLC is said to have raised the chances of spotting an inbound aircraft with the searchlight from 1% to 90%. I put a lot of time into writing this, and I hope that you enjoy reading it. If you can spare a few dollars, consider supporting me on ko-fi . You'll receive an occasional extra, subscribers-only post, and defray the costs of providing artisanal, hand-built world wide web directly from Albuquerque, New Mexico. Consider a typical World War II searchlight, the GE Model 1942, introduced the year that its model number suggests. This 60" searchlight came on a trailer, with a second trailer up to 600 feet away for the 12 kW diesel power plant and the control station up to 300 feet away. What we might now call accessory interfaces allowed the searchlight to receive synchro signals from a locator and send them to a firing computer. These searchlights still required quite a bit of maintenance, and they provided features to ease that work, like a work light inside the searchlight drum for replacing the carbon rods. The Second World War also brought about a renaissance in aerial searchlights. Mostly abandoned in the First World War because of their tendency to attract fire, searchlights returned to aircraft for a decidedly nautical use. Submarines, all diesel-electric during WWII, typically surfaced at night to run their engines and charge their batteries. The first submarine-hunting aircraft used compact carbon arc searchlights to pick submarines out of the dark. The system was remarkably effective, and prompted a change in strategy for diesel submarines, which had to rely on their own anti-aircraft weapons rather than mere stealth. Radar complemented the searchlight, but only for a short time. Radar locators for searchlights were basically an interim measure, making the best use of early radar sets that were sensitive enough to detect aircraft but lacked the spatial resolution to locate them precisely. Radar engineers, especially in Britain, made rapid improvements. For anti-submarine warfare, for example, shortwave radar systems were far more sensitive. It wasn't long before radar could directly guide anti-aircraft weapons, as well. Military searchlights had a role to play all the way through the Korean War, but a much reduced one. Anti-aircraft detection and firing is now firmly the domain of electronic warfare: radio waves, not light beams, search our skies. Surplus Light The declining relevance of searchlights to the military proved an enormous boon to their civilian use. Searchlights were tremendously expensive, so promotional use had been limited to major events like world's fairs. During the war, on the other hand, the Army had built thousands of them. Afterwards, through the War Surplus Administration, it parted with most of them at bargain rates. Entrepreneurial spirits, many of them veterans of the war, purchased secondhand air defense searchlights and offered them for advertising. Just about any auto dealership could afford to hire a searchlight for a sale, and many did. In California, it became traditional for dealerships to bring in searchlights to announce the new model year. There is a bit of moth in every human being, operators of giant searchlights have found. Whenever a searchlight is probing into the night sky, motorists are apt to go blocks, even miles out of their way to track down the source. [^2] Growing up in Portland, I remember seeing strange lights in the sky and searching for their origin. The searchlights utterly fascinated me, even if the source inevitably turned out to be another car lot. In New Mexico, promotional searchlights are rare, although not unheard of. The predominant weather may be a factor, since cloud cover makes searchlights more obvious. But it's mostly a matter of geography: the largest concentration of military searchlights was on the West Coast, and many overseas units were returned to West Coast ports. Los Angeles became the capital of the searchlight because they were cheapest there. There are still WWII military surplus searchlights in promotional use, but far fewer than there once were. Parts are hard to come by, and the operation of carbon arc lamps is a less familiar skill.
